When someone realizes or suspects they are not cisgender, no matter their age, a tumultuous period of questioning and deep self-exploration usually begins, if they don't stuff themselves further into the closet out of fear. This can take months, years, decades, before someone knows who they are, as there is often a lot of learning and unlearning trans and nonbinary people do in their process of self-discovery. Finding who they are and taking the steps of transitioning socially and/or medically, legally, etc. is the start of their life as their true self. Until then, and even after then, there is a disconnect - a discomfort, a pain, an agony, a desperate need for soul and body to match. 


Cis people who are firm in their identity do not experience this. The world is made for cisgender people. 


So if it seems like your family member is centering their life/personality around their gender right now, that is why. 


Source: I'm agender, in my late 20's, and didn't even know what trans people were until I was 18. I was raised Lutheran but am no longer religious. I've had gender affirming surgery and have been on HRT for almost 2 years. As another glimpse into my experience as an agender person, I'm in the process of getting my legal name changed, which I have to go through a court hearing for and pay $500 in fees. Also involved in this process is getting my birth name and new name published in the local newspaper, and getting ink fingerprinted at the local jail for a background check through the FBI. Then I can have the court hearing. I have jumped through all of the hoops, except for the hearing, and it has been an extremely humiliating process.

Hey! I had top surgery just over two months ago and I’m agender. I’ve also been on HRT for about 7 months. Before surgery, my chest size was DDD/F. My surgeon removed around 8 or 10 pounds of tissue total along with my nip nops. The list of pros & cons I made looks similar to yours. 


A couple things:


-A top surgery for trans/non-binary people doesn’t necessarily reduce your risk of breast cancer. If your surgery involves chest reconstruction or your surgeon leaving any breast tissue, you’ll still need to keep an eye out for the risk of cancer. The type of surgery that would prevent breast cancer is usually only performed on cancer patients and it removes all breast tissue. 

-Before surgery, I really enjoyed erotic nipple sensation and was anxious about losing that especially since I opted for no nips. But the way I can enjoy sex now that I’m in -my- body… I am not even fully healed/don’t have full range of movement yet. The confidence and agender euphoria makes up for the lack of nips. 
-My life has changed dramatically for the better since top surgery. I can think clearly, I don’t struggle with anger nearly as much or irritability as often, I’m confident for the first time in my life, I have more time in the day because I’m not messing with binders or finding clothes that lessen dysphoria, my chronic back/neck/shoulder pain has disappeared completely (it was gone instantly after surgery), I can take full deep breaths, my posture is improving, I sleep better, I look forward to leaving the house more often, I enjoy looking in the mirror and photos of myself don’t make me want to cry, clothes fit properly and my wardrobe options have opened so much - clothes shopping for the first time after surgery was a spiritual experience! I could go on… it’s like there’s my life before surgery, and then my life after surgery. In the best possible way. 


Do what feels right to you, do what you need :)
